[Perception] He said it like I simply “chose not to” tell Arun, as if it was a straightforward decision I made lightly. That felt wrong. It misses what was at stake for me — my family’s dignity, my son’s judgment, the whole burden of keeping this contained for thirty years. I did consider it, yes, but not because I was ready to confess or because it would have been right to do. I needed him to understand that this is not a casual omission, not an easy choice, but something I have protected very carefully.

[Decision] I have to correct him. I need to make clear that this is not something he can reduce to me “choosing” silence, as if I simply refused. I am telling him: no one can speak of this. He must understand the seriousness of that demand, because if he treats it like an ordinary secret, he does not understand me at all.

What I can’t quite settle is whether he means I’m identifying with her, or whether he’s suggesting I’m already inside the same pattern she’s enacting. The part that hit me is the idea that a child taking care of a broken parent is not just sad but a kind of reversal, a disordering. That’s the piece I can’t let sit comfortably, because it makes the whole thing feel less like an isolated case with Laura and more like a structure that repeats. If that’s true, then her “escape” may not be only about her father and that older man — it may be about trying to get out of a deadening role before it swallows her.

[Decision] I decided to hold the line on the “unnatural” part because that’s the clearest thing I can say without getting pulled into his theory too quickly. But I also decided, at least internally, not to dismiss the possibility that the same reversal is at work in more than one place. If Laura’s escape is a flight from being made into a parent, then maybe I need to ask what exactly she thinks she is escaping into, and what she’s repeating in the process. I don’t want to concede that this is about me in a simple way, but I can’t ignore that his question is forcing a more general puzzle: why does this kind of reversal create such a powerful need to run, and why does it keep finding the same shapes?

[Perception] They’re saying I could just do more video calls and a virtual catch-up, and honestly that does make sense a bit — but what I’m really hearing is that this whole awful state is being driven by the lockdown and not being able to see people properly. My mood isn’t just randomly bad; it’s this situation, these restrictions, the isolation, and the way everyone else seems to be coping better than me. That’s what hit me. If I’m feeling low, it feels like the circumstances are to blame, not that there’s something fundamentally wrong with me.

[Decision] So I’m going to treat this as a temporary response to being stuck in these conditions. I’ll try the virtual party idea because it sounds practical and it might help, but I’m not going to leap to the conclusion that I’ve got some deeper problem just because I’m struggling now. The real issue is this lockdown life and being cut off from friends, and if I can change that a little, maybe my mood will shift too.

[Perception] She’s actually asking how I’m doing, not just what needs to get done. That lands on the worry I’ve been carrying about the divorce, the kids, and everything staying stable. I can feel how much I’ve been holding in by staying practical.

[Decision] I’m going to be a little more honest and say I’m worried, because I can tell this might be a place where I don’t have to keep all of it to myself. It feels safer to start small than to pretend I’m fine.

context.text: I saw my mom last week for the first time in a while. She took me to brunch. And what did you talk about? My brother.

[Perception] She’s making it sound like this is some huge sign that my mom is completely missing me, like I’m actually neglected in a serious way. But really, it was just brunch. We talked about my brother, which is what we always talk about. And the makeup thing — that was just me trying to look nice, not some big statement about hiding. She’s focusing on the worst possible interpretation, and it’s making this feel bigger than it is.

[Decision] I’m going to keep this small. It’s not like I was in danger or anything; I was just tired and being dramatic. My mom not noticing every little thing doesn’t mean she doesn’t care. If I treat it like a huge problem, then it becomes this whole thing I have to deal with, and I don’t want that. It’s easier to say it wasn’t that serious and move on.

[Perception] They seem to be offering generic “just try this” ideas without really taking in what my situation is actually like. The phone thing doesn’t fit me at all, and the Christmas suggestion feels especially out of touch — as if I could just casually invite someone in and they’d somehow turn around and include me in their family plans. That ignores how private people are here and how much of this is about having a real, in-person connection, not a makeshift workaround. It made me feel like they were tossing out cheerful solutions from a distance, without understanding the social reality I’m dealing with.

[Decision] I’m not going to pretend those ideas are useful just because they sound caring. I’ll answer politely, but I’m mentally setting them aside because they don’t seem grounded in my life. I want something real and local, not a phone chat or a hopeful guess about people suddenly making room for me. If that’s all they can offer, then I need to stay guarded and not get pulled into acting like it’s a serious answer.

Unemployment won’t cover my bills, my contract is ending, and there isn’t another offer waiting. It lands on the part of me that feels like I’m already behind, already losing ground, and there’s no simple fix. The more we talk about coping and mindset, the more it feels like I’m being asked to make myself okay with something that isn’t okay.

[Decision] I think I’m just going to stop pushing for a solution right now, because every option I can see feels too small or too uncertain. If I keep reaching for hope, I’ll just set myself up to feel worse when it doesn’t work out. It feels safer to admit I can’t deal with this at the moment and not force myself to pretend I can.

The encouragement helps a little, but it doesn’t tell me how to actually focus when I’m nervous and distracted.

[Decision] I decided to ask directly for advice because I need something concrete I can use right away. If I only hint that I’m struggling, I might just get reassurance again, and I need strategies that help me manage my attention and anxiety while I study. Asking plainly feels like the fastest way to get useful help without making it a bigger emotional conversation than I can handle right now.

text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] She’s trying to make my father’s visits and the candies and the piano into proof that I was abandoned, that I was a kid who wanted to come home and got left anyway. She’s also saying I gave her the cassette because I wanted her to understand the 10-year-old me and maybe change her mind about me. That’s the part that hit: if she sees me as someone who was just lonely and wanted to stay, then all the blame I’ve been carrying starts to wobble. And if I let that happen, then I have to feel how much it hurt that nobody took me home.

[Decision] No. I’m not going there. I was difficult. I know I was. That’s the line I’m drawing because if I stop saying it was my fault, then I have to admit I was sent away and nobody came for me, and I can’t afford that. Better to stay with the version where I was impossible than to open the door to being the kind of child who was wanted and still left behind.

[Perception] They’re making it sound like I’m supposed to treat this like some huge life crisis with a bunch of rules and stages, but maybe it doesn’t have to be that intense. Yeah, it sucks, and I’m hurt, but it’s still just a breakup. My life got shaken up, sure, but not destroyed. They’re focusing on all these feelings and big emotional frameworks, and that just makes it feel bigger than I want to admit. Maybe I’m not actually as stuck as this sounds.

[Decision] I’m going to tell myself to keep it in perspective and not let it become some massive thing. I can be upset without acting like my whole future is ruined. If I stay busy, work out, and keep my routine simple, this will probably settle down on its own. I don’t need to make it more serious than it is.

[Perception] The therapist just asked me to tell him my problems, plain and simple, so I figured I should lay out the actual setup instead of talking around it. What felt important was the chain of how we all ended up here: the ex, the woman from the apartment, the marriage, and now the ex living next door. I wanted it to come across that this isn’t some abstract issue — it’s an ongoing neighborhood mess with real awkward run-ins, and it’s mostly because these two women can’t seem to be around each other without tension.

[Decision] So I decided to give the whole backstory in order, because I wanted the therapist to see that the awkwardness makes sense once you understand the history. I’m basically saying: this is the situation, it’s complicated, and I don’t really know what a fix would even be besides everybody getting along, which doesn’t seem very realistic. I’m hoping he’ll get that it’s more of a live-with-it kind of thing than a simple problem to solve.

[Perception] She’s still talking like this is just a matter of time and routines, like if I keep showing up and forcing myself into places with the kids, something good will happen. That’s exactly what hurts — the idea that I’m supposed to open myself up again after last year, after thinking I had something and losing it. “You won’t be alone for long” doesn’t feel comforting; it feels like pressure. It means risking wanting someone, being seen, and getting disappointed again. I can hear the assumption that I should be trying to find another chance, and I don’t want that. I want the quiet. I want control. I don’t want to feel stupid for hoping.

[Decision] No. I’m not doing that again. I’m drawing the line here: I’m not taking another risk just to end up embarrassed, hurt, or hoping for something I can’t keep. I can handle being alone better than I can handle being let down. I’m not going to build my life around another chance at love. I’d rather stay with what I know than go back into that.

[Perception] I heard the therapist trying to get me to look at hobbies, treats, and little ways to feel better, and I know they mean well. But what I was really holding onto was the idea that I’m not completely alone in this, that I still have my aunt to look forward to and that maybe the new meds can help when nothing else has. What hit me most was how empty and flat everything feels even when I’m doing the “right” things. I can walk, knit, stay grateful, and still not feel joy. That scares me, because it makes me feel broken in a way I don’t know how to fix.

[Decision] I decided to keep it polite and grateful and not push into the darker part of how hard this really is. I want to keep the focus on hope—on my aunt, on the medication, on thankfulness—because if I let the sadness take up all the space, I’m afraid I’ll sound ungrateful or burden everyone with how bad it feels. It seemed safer to end with blessing them and move on than to say how hopeless I still feel underneath.

[Perception] What I heard was: this is all about some lost version of me, some old innocence I can’t get back. That landed right on the part that already hurts — that Leah knew me before I got guarded, before everything got complicated, before I shut people out. And if that’s what this is, then it’s not really about the lateness or the missed plans at all. It’s about a thing that’s already gone. That’s what feels depressing: not just that she disappoints me, but that the only person who knew me that way belongs to a past I can’t return to.

[Decision] So I’m going to shut this down. If I let myself hope this means something fixable, I’ll just end up wanting what I can’t have — the old kind of being known, the easy kind of love, the version of me that existed before I had to protect myself. Better to call it depressing and leave it there. At least then I don’t have to reach for something that’s already been lost.

[Perception] They were talking like this was just a simple communication problem, like I could fix heartbreak with some neat little suggestion. It felt like they were not really hearing how impossible everything is for me — deaf girlfriend, no hands, and now they want to act like “just talk to her” is some genius answer. That rubbed me the wrong way because it made me feel stupid, like my whole life is some obvious puzzle they can solve from the outside without knowing what it costs me. It also felt like they were missing the point that I’m already doing everything I can, and the failure is still being laid at my feet.

[Decision] So I shut it down. If they’re going to come at me with useless, obvious stuff, then I’m not going to act impressed by it. I decided to answer in a way that shows how absurd their advice sounds in my situation, because honestly I need them to see this isn’t some ordinary relationship problem. If they can’t grasp that, then I don’t trust them enough to take their suggestions seriously.

context.speaker: therapist

text_bundle.therapist_turn: Just listening to you talk I can tell this is something that is making you extremely anxious.

text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] I heard that she could tell how anxious this is for me, and that landed because it means I’m not totally hiding it even when I’m trying to. When I said I “freeze and ramble,” I was touching the part I’m most ashamed of — that I can’t stay organized enough to explain something so important, and then I worry I’m making my spouse overwhelmed or pulling him away from me. Saying “very much so” was me admitting how intense the fear is: not just fear of the story itself, but fear of what it might do to how he sees me.

[Decision] I decided to say a little more truthfully instead of trying to sound okay, because I’m tired of pretending this is just a simple conversation problem. I wanted her to understand that the panic is taking over before I can even get the words out, and that the real risk I feel is losing my husband’s view of me. Saying it out loud felt safer than trying to force myself to explain everything at once.

text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] He answered the question too cleanly, like he was trying to pin me down instead of meeting the point. “You mean if I said yes?” made it sound simple, almost clinical, but what hit me was that he was refusing to play along with the fantasy I was offering. I was trying to see whether he’d step out of the professional frame and admit there’s something real in wanting to bend it for me — not because I actually need that, but because if he did, then this would stop feeling so one-sided and sterile. His response made me feel like he was putting the burden right back on me, as if I’m the one asking for the impossible while pretending that’s not what I’m doing.

[Decision] So I pushed it into the open: “So you want to?” I said it to force a plain answer, to stop the careful hovering and make him show his hand. If he says yes, then I’m not the only one playing this game. If he says no, then at least we’re finally naming that he’s choosing the rules, not just hiding behind them. Either way, I wanted to see whether there’s any truth here beyond the script, because I’m tired of pretending the distance itself is somehow helpful.

I don’t really feel worthy of starting over, and I don’t see how anything I do could bring back what I lost.

[Decision] I decided to stop reaching for hope because hoping just makes the loss hurt more. If I don’t let myself believe in a new future, then I don’t have to face failing at it too. It feels safer to stay numb, to keep my expectations low, and to just exist through this instead of trying to build something I’m not sure I can have.

I needed to correct him and make it clear that I did not deliberately orchestrate some dramatic message with being late — I was late because life happened, and I’m already dealing with enough without being accused of having some secret plan. That comparison feels unfair and insulting, and it misses what I’m actually trying to do: get through saying something I can barely say at all. text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] She’s trying to connect the timing of Natalie leaving with when the insomnia started, but she won’t just make it a simple cause-and-effect statement. What I hear is: she thinks there may be a connection, but she’s not willing to reduce it to “your daughter left, therefore you can’t sleep.” That lands on the part of me that’s trying to keep this clean and practical. If I can identify the mechanism, then maybe I can deal with it. If it’s just vague emotional fallout, then I’m back to sitting here being told it’s anxiety when I don’t experience it that way. I’m also hearing that she’s testing whether I’m willing to look at this as more than a sleep problem, and that feels like a question I need answered before I can decide whether this conversation is useful.

[Decision] I’m going to push her to be more specific. If it’s not “one-on-one” between Natalie and the insomnia, then what is it? Stress about the move? Regret about the decision? Something about responsibility, or loss, or the fact that I didn’t say no when she wanted me to? I want a model that makes sense, not a hand-wave. If she can’t explain why she thinks this connection matters, then I’m not going to accept it just because it sounds psychologically tidy. But if there is a real chain here, I want to understand it, because otherwise I’m just chasing sleep without knowing what’s actually keeping me awake.

It feels impossible, and trying to imagine doing it just makes me want to disappear into silence.

[Decision] I’m not going to do this right now. I can’t. There’s no point forcing myself into something that will break me open and hurt her too. I know I’ll probably leave here and still not be able to say it, and that feels like the truth of it: I don’t have the strength to make this real for her. [Decision] So I snapped at him. If he’s going to act clueless at the exact moment I’m trying to be honest, then I’m not going to be gracious about it. I want him to feel how irritating and alienating that was, because if he can’t even recognize the basic shape of what I’m saying, then he doesn’t get to stand there like the wise one. It ignores how much influence I actually have in the room, and it flattens the way therapy can stir things up, not just clarify them. He was acting like understanding is always enough and always good, when I know that forcing too much consciousness can overwhelm a person and leave them less able to function. It also felt like he was turning the whole thing into a moral claim about therapists being responsible for outcomes in a way I don’t accept.

[Decision] I decided I had to push back because I didn’t want his version to stand as if it were the whole truth. I needed to correct the idea that therapy is simply “understand and then whatever happens isn’t our fault,” and I needed to make clear that I don’t buy the fantasy that making everything conscious is automatically healing. I’m testing whether that old truth still fits, or whether I’m forcing it to stand in for what I’m feeling now. I need to compare then and now honestly — not by what I’m “supposed” to choose, but by what I can actually live with. [Perception] He’s trying to hand me something I can’t use. “Your son loved you.” “He admired you.” That lands right on the wound I keep pressed shut. Because if that’s true, then all the years of hard edges, all the pushing and correcting and tightening the screws… it didn’t even buy me honesty. It just bought me a son who kept giving and giving. And I can see what he’s doing: trying to make this hurt less, trying to turn it into something clean. But it isn’t clean. It’s just me standing there, realizing I made a life out of force and called it care. If I let myself believe he loved me, then I have to live with the fact that I didn’t know what to do with it. I don’t know what to do with that.

[Decision] So no, I’m not taking that comfort. I’d rather stay with the ugliness of it, because at least that matches what I can bear to believe. If I accept that he admired me, then maybe I have to admit the whole thing wasn’t some necessary hardness, some noble damage. Maybe it was just me, being too much, too controlling, too late to matter. And what’s the point of hoping now? The years are already spent. The boy is already grown. I can’t go back and give him a different father. I can’t undo the way I trained him to disappear himself for me. So I’ll sit with the thing I know how to survive: that I deserved to be hated, and that if he loved me anyway, then that only makes the waste of it worse.

text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] The therapist is asking about talking to her, but that misses the real thing. She is deaf, so normal talking is not the issue. The problem is not me not trying hard enough — it is that I cannot communicate like other people can, and that made everything go wrong. Her ex had hands and could do things I cannot. That is what hurt me and what got used against me.

[Decision] I am not going to take the blame for this. I did not cause her cheating — my body did not fail her, she chose to do that. The real problem is my disability and the fact that she went back to someone who could give her what I could not. If I had hands, she would not have had to cheat. I need to hold onto that because otherwise it just feels like I am the one who is broken.

context.text: Well, let's try to take it one problem at a time so's not to get overwhelmed. What is your biggest problem at the moment?

text_bundle.therapist_turn: Ah, am I to take it that a relationship has recently ended?
text_bundle.client_response: When we met, before we got involved, he said he was divorced. I ended up finding out that he was still legally married. He assured me that they were just a pen's stroke away from being divorced.
text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] He’s asking me to narrow it down, and I can feel how big this all is. What’s weighing on me most is that I thought I was building something honest, and instead he started it by lying about the most basic thing: whether he was even available. I needed the therapist to understand that this wasn’t a small detail or a misunderstanding — he told me he was divorced, and that turned out not to be true. When I said he was “a pen’s stroke away” from divorce, I was trying to show how he made it sound almost finished, almost resolved, like there was nothing real to worry about.

[Decision] I decided to lay out the history plainly because I’m trying to decide whether trust can ever come back after this. If the therapist understands how it started, maybe it’ll be clearer why I feel so stuck — because I’m not just upset about one lie, I’m questioning the whole foundation of the relationship and whether I can believe anything he says now.

context.speaker: client
context.text: What does the good therapist do when the patient needs more than just... talk? Do you just sit there and listen until she dies on the couch?

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: You can only be responsible for what happens in treatment. You know that.

text_bundle.therapist_turn: You can only be responsible for what happens in treatment. You know that.

text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] I heard: “Stay in your lane. Limit yourself to the treatment room. Don’t reach for more.” It hit the worst part of this: April is refusing treatment and I’m watching someone I think may die, and the message back is that my hands are tied. It felt like my concern was being reduced to a role issue, as if the moral emergency here is just an overstep to be managed. What felt intolerable was the idea that “being a good therapist” means doing nothing while someone slips away.

[Decision] No. I’m not going to pretend that’s enough. I’m not going to turn this into some neat boundary lesson and let the patient die while I sit there and call it ethics. I won’t take her to chemo, and I won’t cross that line — but I also won’t accept being told that helplessness is the only proper response. If that’s all this room can offer, then I’m not going there. I draw the line at being asked to make peace with abandonment.

I know there’s something I’m supposed to do, but I don’t really want to deal with all the details or admit I’m not on top of it. If I go deeper, I’d have to say I’m confused, maybe ask for help, and probably look like I haven’t been paying attention. That feels annoying and kind of embarrassing.

[Decision] I’m going to keep it short and vague so I don’t have to commit to anything or get pushed into explaining more than I want to. “I’m not sure” lets me sound cooperative without having to take responsibility for figuring it out right now. It feels safer to stay light than to open the whole thing up and have to admit I’m lost or that I haven’t really done anything yet.

What I was trying to get across is that this isn’t some random fight — it cost me the relationship. Nina and I are basically done because of it. And the part that matters is that I brought her into my life because she seemed to get Oliver, seemed like she’d be with me in this. Instead, it feels like she picked a side against me. That’s what stings: I thought she’d be an ally, and now it looks like she was never really on my side.

[Decision] So I decided to lay it out plainly, because I want the therapist to see the bigger picture — not just that there was a fight, but that I lost Nina over something I thought she understood. I’m trying to show that I wasn’t out there with some random woman; I had a reason for choosing her, and that reason blew up in my face. I need it understood that what happened feels like betrayal, not just disagreement.

But I don’t want to sit with that discomfort, so I’m telling myself this is mostly coming from outside her—peer pressure, rebelliousness, the influence of others—not from me or from a deeper issue between us.

[Decision] I’m going to frame this as her being a good girl who’s being pushed around by other kids, because that feels safer than admitting I don’t know how to manage this or that I may need to look at my own role. If it’s peer pressure, then the real problem is the outside influence, and I can keep seeing myself as the protective father trying to fix what’s affecting her.

[Decision] So I should keep it light and manageable. I can mention it in a small way, but I don’t need to make it into this big emotional issue. It’s better to act like I’m handling it okay and not overstate how hard it is. If I keep it contained, I won’t make anyone uncomfortable, and it won’t become this bigger thing than it has to be.

[Decision] No. I’m not taking that frame. “Dangerous” and “weak” aren’t my father’s words, and I’m not going to make him into somebody who couldn’t bear his own life. That would feel like betraying him. So I shut it down: that’s just his way. It works for him. I don’t know if it’s mine, but I’m not letting you turn it into some problem he’s hiding under.

[Decision] So I kept it small and practical: “I have major decisions to make.” That lets me stay in control and keeps the conversation on logistics instead of need. It’s safer to sound like I’m thinking than to admit I’m hoping. If I go deeper, I might sound needy, or find out I’m alone in this, and I can’t afford that right now.

It also hit the fear underneath it, that if I admit that side exists, then it means I’m weak in a way I can’t fix.

[Decision] I decided not to pretend I didn’t understand her. I corrected her because I’m tired of being treated like I’m vague or stupid, and saying “I know what susceptible means” lets me keep some control. But then I said “I hate that part of me” because that’s the truth I’m closest to right now. I’m willing to touch the hate, even if I’m not ready to touch what’s under it, because saying it out loud feels safer than letting it stay hidden.

context.text: I'm so sad all the time.

context.speaker: therapist

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Have you any history of depression before?

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Have you seen any physicians about the problem?

text_bundle.therapist_turn: Have you seen any physicians about the problem?
text_bundle.client_response: Maybe I should make an appointment.
text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] The therapist wasn’t pushing me or making me feel like I was being labeled, just asking whether I’d seen a physician. Hearing that made this feel a little more ordinary and manageable, like maybe sadness this constant is something worth checking out instead of just trying to carry alone. It hit the part of me that’s been worried this is starting to take up too much space in my life.

[Decision] I’m not ready to make a big deal out of it, but I can take one practical step: make an appointment and see what a doctor says. If there’s something they can help with, I want to know. I still want to handle things myself as much as I can, but I’m willing to ask for help now rather than keep hoping it goes away.

context.text: Okay, coach.

text_bundle.therapist_turn: Okay, coach.
text_bundle.client_response: Sorry.
text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] He’s pointing at the same thing I’ve been trying to dodge: that maybe this isn’t some impossible body mystery, maybe it’s food, consistency, and me not wanting to admit I’m off. And he’s doing it in a way that makes me look like the one giving the lecture, which stings because that’s exactly what I do when I don’t want to sit with it. If I stay with that too long, I have to hear how much of this is on me, and then I’m not the freak with special physiology anymore — I’m just the guy who isn’t getting the results.

[Decision] So I kept it short and called him “coach,” like I was playing along instead of actually accepting it. That’s safer. If I say more, I might have to agree, and agreeing means losing the shield of sarcasm and uniqueness. I don’t want to hand over control, and I don’t want to hear myself admit he might be right. Brevity lets me retreat without openly fighting him.

context.speaker: client
context.text: My friend thinks we should still be friends but her drug addict boyfriend has already borrowed money from myself and others too many times and has stolen from other people.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Let me see if I understand you correctly, you no longer want to be friends because her boyfriend is a drug addict and a thief?

context.speaker: client
context.text: Yes, I can still care about her but I cannot be a part of her life if this is what she wants.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: i can understand and i have had to do the same thing.

text_bundle.therapist_turn: i can understand and i have had to do the same thing.
text_bundle.client_response: Am I wrong? Sometimes I'm confused by what I'm seeing. Other times, like now, I feel confident in my decision. I guess I never thought I would see her end up with this kind of situation.
text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] I heard the therapist saying they understand, and that they’ve had to make a similar choice themselves. That landed on the part of me that is torn between caring about my friend and not wanting to keep being pulled into her boyfriend’s behavior. What still feels unresolved is whether stepping back makes me a bad friend, or whether it’s actually the clearest way to protect myself from being used, lied to, or dragged into more chaos. I’m also noticing the gap between who I thought my friend was and what her life looks like now. That’s what I’m trying to make sense of: how someone I’ve known for so long could end up in this situation, and whether I’m supposed to keep showing up anyway.

[Decision] I decided I need to keep the boundary, even if I hate it. I’m not deciding to stop caring about her; I’m deciding that caring doesn’t have to mean staying close while money, trust, and safety are being damaged. I want to stay open to the idea that she may one day get away from him, but I can’t base my actions on hope alone. Right now the more responsible choice seems to be stepping back and letting the reality of her choices be hers to live with, because I can’t fix this for her and I can’t afford to keep absorbing the consequences.

[Perception] I heard the therapist asking if I invest, and that made me feel like I should explain the bigger picture instead of just giving a yes or no. I’m a student, so it’s not like I’m some full-time trader or anything — I just try to put as much money as I can into the market. Saying that out loud was my way of showing that this is part of how I manage things and why the market being down is on my mind, even though I’m still feeling better than usual.

[Decision] I decided to be straightforward and give a little context so it wouldn’t sound like I was making a big deal out of nothing. I wanted the therapist to understand that investing is something I fit into my life as a student, and that even when I’m doing okay, stuff like the market still affects me in the background.

context.speaker: client
context.text: Look... I lost Izzy a long time ago. But Russell, that... That was a bit of a shock.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: When did you separate?

context.speaker: client
context.text: Two years ago. He had an affair.

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Yes, you said, with one of his students.

text_bundle.therapist_turn: Yes, you said, with one of his students.
text_bundle.client_response: Oh God, what a cliché, huh? I was faithful. I had a lot of jobs out of town. Many opportunities, but I resisted. He had to go and piss all over everything. Can I tell you something that I haven't told anyone?
text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] He keeps it plain, almost clinical: “two years ago,” “an affair,” “with one of his students.” It lands on the part of me that wants this to be simple, one clean explanation, because then I can keep standing on the high ground. I was faithful. I resisted. I did what I was supposed to do, even when I was away a lot. And yet here I am, two years later, still feeling like the whole thing was torn apart by something cheap and obvious. What I’m circling around is this: if I was the one who did everything “right,” then why does it still feel like I lost something I don’t know how to replace? And why am I suddenly thinking of telling him something I’ve never said out loud?

[Decision] I decided to say there’s something I haven’t told anyone because I want to test whether there’s more to this than just his betrayal and my outrage. If I say it out loud, maybe I can figure out whether I’m talking about the marriage, or the loneliness after it, or the fact that I’ve been acting as if I don’t need anything anymore. I’m still protecting myself by sounding sarcastic and in control, but underneath that I’m wondering if there’s a reason I’m bringing this up now — whether I’m looking for a way to explain why I’ve stayed shut down for so long, and whether I can admit that without giving up my dignity.

context.speaker: client
context.text: How many people come to you with like a really big problem?

context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Like what?

text_bundle.therapist_turn: Like what?
text_bundle.client_response: I don't know... A death, a rape. I don't know.
text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] She’s asking what “big problem” means, and I can feel her trying to get closer to the thing I’m circling. I brought up the worst examples because that’s safer than saying the actual thing. If I say it plainly, it becomes real, and then I’d have to deal with all the fear and shame and whatever else comes with it. And I already have too much in my head with this project hanging over me.

[Decision] So I’m keeping it vague on purpose. If I say “I don’t know,” I’m still answering, but I’m not opening the door all the way. Brevity feels safer because it lets me stay in control, not get flooded, and not have to explain the thing I’m not ready to say out loud.

text_bundle.therapist_turn: Have you considered doing meditation to release negative thoughts?

text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] When they brought up meditation like it was a simple solution, it felt like they were glossing over how overwhelmed I actually am. I heard it as “just calm yourself down,” and that didn’t fit what I’m dealing with. I’m not only upset in a general way — I’m hurt, stuck thinking about the breakup, and already having a hard time focusing on anything. So it felt off-base, like it missed the real issue and assumed I could just switch my mind off.

[Decision] I wanted to push back because I don’t want them to treat this like a small stress problem with a quick fix. I needed to make it clear that I’ve already looked into ideas like that, and the problem is that I can’t even settle enough to use them right now. In my head, I was thinking: that may help some people, but it doesn’t touch what I’m feeling today, and I need them to understand that before suggesting another tool.

[Perception] He was drifting away from the thing that actually matters to me and back into his questions, like the spilled soda and the train ride were the whole story. At that moment I wanted him to see that this was not about the train at all — it was about what I was carrying home, what was waiting for me there, and whether he understood why I was already spent before I even walked in.

[Decision] So I cut in and asked, “How things are at home?” instead of waiting for him to guess. I put it into words because hinting would not get me anywhere, and I did not want another round of him asking about the train when what I needed was for the conversation to turn toward home — toward whatever is actually weighing on me. I am trying to steer this, not just endure it.

text_bundle.internal:
[Perception] He’s doing it again — turning my pain into a story about my family, about my father, about my mother, like I’m just a repeat of them. And he said it like he knew what I “wanted,” like he could name my loss better than I can. It hit the part where I already feel weak and stupid for needing help at all. If I stay in this conversation, I’m going to be told that my bed, my shutting down, my anger, all of it means something ugly about me and my family. That feels intolerable.

[Decision] No. I’m not going deeper into this with him. I’m drawing the line here because I do not want my grief explained away as family pathology, and I do not want to be made to sit there and pick myself apart just to prove I’m healing. If therapy means feeling worse, feeling exposed, and losing the one thing I have left — my toughness, my distance, my ability to function — then I’m done. I can get through the day on my own. I have to.

[Decision] I’m not going to keep digging into that with her. I won’t sit here and pick apart the one thing I’ve already destroyed just because she wants me to look at it differently. I can’t change what I did, and I’m not going to pretend I can. I’d rather stop here than keep going into that pain.

[Decision] No. I’m not going there. I’ll keep this on the surface where it belongs—money, lessons, family logistics, pierogis, protocol. I can be the aunt who pays for the music, not the woman who falls apart talking about what music meant to her. I’m not handing over that part of myself in this room.

If I let myself agree that it’s enormous, then I have to act like everything is at risk, and I’m not willing to go there. Better to keep it in perspective, minimize the drama, and hold onto the belief that this is temporary and not as bad as he’s making it sound.

I wanted him to see that my father wasn’t just absent in a dramatic way; he was there in the monthly check, in the formalities, in the money, while the actual family was left to absorb the damage.

I was trying to pin down whether she’d acknowledge Laura at all, whether she’d tell me what kind of relationship there was, and whether she’d finally admit there was something improper here. [Decision] I decided to answer the way I did because I need to test that premise out loud: that I didn’t just make a mistake, I outsourced my judgment and ignored what I already knew. Saying “like a novice” is me trying to locate the failure precisely — not just “I was wrong,” but “I betrayed my own clinical sense.” I’m trying to figure out if the real problem is that I trusted the advice itself, or that I let the need to be guided override the part of me that was warning me not to. If I don’t expect anything good, maybe it will hurt less if the worst happens. I know that means I’m shutting down, but it feels safer than opening my heart and risking losing this baby, my partner, and whatever is left of me all at once.
